query: For high-entropy alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict the observations relative to a baseline, state the limits within which the hypothesis should hold, identify evidence that would support it, and specify an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the degree of local chemical order (LCO) via controlled annealing elevates yield strength and hardness by raising dislocation activation barriers through a rugged local energy landscape.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic NiCoCr medium-entropy alloy in a near-random solid-solution state with uniform and controlled fine grain size.
generation.intervention: Apply a series of annealing treatments at varied temperatures and durations designed to promote different degrees of LCO (e.g., low-temperature, long-duration annealing) while monitoring and controlling grain growth and phase purity.
generation.conditions: Samples annealed in identical atmospheres with only temperature/time varied; post-anneal microstructure to be verified by XRD, TEM, and EBSD; mechanical tests performed at room temperature and identical strain rates.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced LCO evidenced by variations in pairwise short-range order parameters measured using atom probe tomography or X-ray scattering, with concurrent confirmation of constant grain size.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced LCO modifies the local energy landscape by increasing localized planar fault energies, which elevates the activation barriers for dislocation motion and forces dislocations to overcome a more rugged path, thereby increasing strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The sample with enhanced LCO is expected to exhibit a ~15–25% increase in yield strength and hardness relative to the rapidly quenched, disordered baseline.
generation.baseline: An HEA in a near-random (disordered) state achieved by rapid quenching, with uniform grain size and no significant LCO.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is applicable to FCC HEAs processed under conditions that avoid phase separation and significant grain growth; at very high temperatures or under conditions where diffusion dominates, the LCO effect may be obscured.
generation.uncertainty: While increased LCO is linked to higher activation barriers for dislocation motion, concurrent effects such as minor grain growth or segregation may affect results; this is addressed by comprehensive microstructural characterization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of NiCoCr HEA samples: one subjected to a long-duration, lower-temperature anneal (to enhance LCO) and one rapidly quenched to retain disorder. Characterize grain size and phase purity with XRD and EBSD, then perform in-situ mechanical testing while assessing LCO via APT or X-ray scattering.
measurements: Pairwise short-range order parameters via APT or X-ray scattering
In-situ observations of dislocation nucleation via TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed (LCO-enhanced) sample does not demonstrate a statistically significant (15–25%) increase in yield strength or hardness relative to the quenched sample, or if increased LCO does not correlate with higher dislocation activation barriers, the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: SignificanceWhile high-entropy alloys (HEAs) or complex concentrated alloys are touted as potential game changer alloys, many fundamental gaps remain in our understanding of these alloys. In particular, the local atomic distributions and their propensity for chemical ordering in HEAs have garnered much interest recently. Conceptually, our paper shows that systematic control of the nature and qualitative extent of ordering in HEAs is possible, starting from simple thermodynamic binary heats of mixing considerations and correlating that with corresponding mechanical properties. This opens the intriguing possibility that thermodynamics can provide excellent a priori guidance to explore the immense compositional space and select suitable alloying elements to discover HEAs with controlled chemical ordering, exhibiting outstanding mechanical properties.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, thermodynamics, chemical ordering AbstractUnderstanding the local chemical ordering propensity in random solid solutions, and tailoring its strength, can guide the design and discovery of complex, paradigm-shifting multicomponent alloys. First, we present a simple thermodynamic framework, based solely on bina

High-entropy and medium-entropy alloys are presumed to have a configurational entropy as high as that of an ideally mixed solid solution (SS) of multiple elements in near-equal proportions. However, enthalpic interactions inevitably render such chemically disordered SSs rare and metastable, except at very high temperatures. Here we highlight the wide variety of local chemical ordering (LCO) that sets these concentrated SSs apart from traditional solvent-solute ones. Using atomistic simulations, we reveal that the LCO of the multi-principal-element NiCoCr SS changes with alloy processing conditions, producing a wide range of generalized planar fault energies. We show that the LCO heightens the ruggedness of the energy landscape and raises activation barriers governing dislocation activities. This influences the selection of dislocation pathways in slip, faulting, and twinning, and increases the lattice friction to dislocation motion via a nanoscale segment detrapping mechanism. In contrast, severe plastic deformation reduces the LCO towards random SS. Multi-principal-element alloys have been assumed to have the configurational entropy of an ideal solution. papers.title: Heterogeneous lattice strain strengthening in severely distorted crystalline solids.
papers.approach: A combined experimental and three‐dimensional discrete dislocation dynamics simulation study that incorporates experimentally measured heterogeneous lattice strain fields.
papers.findings: The work shows that the heterogeneous lattice strain field, arising from severe atomic lattice distortion, contributes significantly to enhanced strength and ductility by impeding dislocation motion and promoting dislocation entanglements.
papers.mechanism: Heterogeneous strain-induced dislocation pinning and sluggish dislocation slip that leads to increased strain hardening and strength.

papers.title: Dislocation flow turbulence simultaneously enhances strength and ductility.
papers.system: Multi‐principal element alloys (MPEAs) including chemically complex, distorted solids
papers.approach: Atomic-scale discrete dislocation dynamics simulations based on a random field theory coupled with phenomenological models to capture atomic-lattice-distortion effects and chemical short-range order.
papers.findings: The study identifies a unique dislocation turbulence induced by heterogeneous lattice strain and chemical short-range order (SRO), which enhances both strength and ductility. This turbulence produces rapid, localized dislocation multiplication and traps at vortex points.
papers.mechanism: SRO-induced heterogeneous lattice strain fields create localized stress peaks that trigger turbulent dislocation motion, effectively acting as both a source and trap for dislocations.

papers.title: Strengthening Mechanisms in CoCrFeNiX₀.₄ (Al, Nb, Ta) High Entropy Alloys Fabricated by Powder Plasma Arc Additive Manufacturing.
papers.system: CoCrFeNi-based HEAs with various additional elements (Al, Nb, Ta)
papers.approach: Experimental investigation via powder plasma arc additive manufacturing coupled with microstructural and mechanical property analyses.
papers.findings: The results indicate that while conventional mechanisms like precipitation, grain boundary, and dislocation strengthening are active, the addition of large-size atoms (e.g., Ta) promotes significant lattice distortion and local eutectic structures that enhance dislocation pinning.
papers.mechanism: Synergistic effect of solid solution (lattice distortion) and dislocation as well as grain boundary strengthening, with local microstructural features (e.g., formation of low-angle grain boundaries) further retarding dislocation motion.

papers.title: Strengthening in multi-principal element alloys with local-chemical-order roughened dislocation pathways.
papers.approach: Large-scale atomistic simulations combining molecular dynamics (MD) and Monte Carlo (MC) techniques to simulate effects of varying local chemical order (LCO) under different annealing conditions.
papers.findings: The presence and variability of local chemical order create a rugged energy landscape that raises activation barriers for dislocation movement. This variability is shown to influence dislocation pathways, stacking fault energies, and overall deformation modes.
papers.mechanism: Local chemical ordering (or its reduction toward a random solid solution) modulates the energy barriers for dislocation slip, resulting in roughened dislocation paths and a nanoscale segment detrapping process that enhances strength.

papers.title: Maximum strength and dislocation patterning in multi-principal element alloys.
papers.system: CrCoNi alloy as a model MPEA
papers.approach: Large-scale atomistic simulations to probe deformation mechanisms and dislocation patterning under given strain rates.
papers.findings: The model reveals that the presence of chemical short-range order increases maximum strength by elevating the barriers for dislocation motion and reducing faulting and transformation. It also shows that dislocation patterns (e.g., planar slip, strain localization) depend on grain orientation and active slip systems.
papers.mechanism: Interplay between SRO and dislocation motion, where SRO increases local resistance (via creating antiphase boundaries and modifying stacking fault energies) to dislocation glide.

papers.title: Fluctuations in local shear-fault energy produce unique and dominating strengthening in metastable complex concentrated alloys.
papers.system: Metastable complex concentrated alloys (e.g., NiCoCr-based CCAs)
papers.approach: Molecular dynamics simulations analyzing local shear-fault energy distributions and their effect on dislocation configurations.
papers.findings: Strength in these alloys is dominated by local fluctuations in shear-fault energy rather than average values. The existence of hard atomic motifs leads to pinning of dislocations and a characteristic ‘wavy’ dislocation configuration.
papers.mechanism: Local fluctuations in shear-fault energy create variable pinning sites for dislocations. This mechanism emphasizes the role of spatial fault energy variation over the globally averaged short-range order.

papers.title: Exceptional enhancement of mechanical properties in high-entropy alloys via thermodynamically guided local chemical ordering.
papers.system: High-entropy alloys selected via thermodynamic binary mixing insights
papers.approach: A thermodynamic framework based on binary heats of mixing to predict and then experimentally tailor local chemical ordering in HEAs to control mechanical properties.
papers.findings: Systematic control of local chemical order via thermodynamic guidance results in HEAs with outstanding mechanical properties. The work suggests that the degree and nature of chemical ordering can be used to predict and design strength.
papers.mechanism: Thermodynamically driven local chemical order modulates dislocation motion by altering activation barriers, thereby directly influencing hardness and yield strength.

established: HEA strength and hardness are strongly influenced by heterogeneous lattice distortions arising from atomic size mismatches and chemical short-range order.
Multiple strengthening mechanisms are active in HEAs, including solid solution, grain boundary, precipitation, and dislocation-based mechanisms.
Local atomic arrangements (e.g., LCO) and fluctuations in local energy landscapes (such as shear-fault energy) play critical roles in determining dislocation mobility.

approaches_tried.approach: Three-dimensional discrete dislocation dynamics simulations incorporating measured heterogeneous strain fields.
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated that heterogeneous lattice strain effectively impedes dislocation motion and enhances strength.

approaches_tried.approach: Atomistic simulations (MD and MC) to quantify the effects of local chemical order on dislocation slip and faulting.
approaches_tried.outcome: Revealed that variable local chemical ordering creates a rugged energy landscape which modifies dislocation pathways and increases strength.

approaches_tried.approach: Experimental studies via additive manufacturing (PPA-AM) with microstructural analysis.
approaches_tried.outcome: Identified contributions of grain boundary, dislocation, and solid solution strengthening in modifying the overall mechanical response.

approaches_tried.approach: Molecular dynamics simulations evaluating local shear-fault energy fluctuations.
approaches_tried.outcome: Showed that local fluctuations rather than averaged properties dominate the pinning behavior, correlating with ultra-high strength.

mechanisms: Heterogeneous lattice strain-induced dislocation pinning and entanglement
Dislocation flow turbulence resulting from chemical short-range order
Local fluctuations in shear-fault energy creating variable pinning sites for dislocations
Modulation of generalized planar fault energies via local chemical ordering
disagreements: Relative contributions of solid solution strengthening versus dislocation-related mechanisms vary between studies.
The importance of average lattice distortion versus local fluctuations (or local chemical order) in governing dislocation mobility is debated.
Differing interpretations on whether grain boundary effects or intrinsic dislocation dynamics (e.g., turbulence, antidote to slip) predominantly set the strength baseline.
open_questions: How can the individual contributions from heterogeneous lattice strain and local chemical order be quantitatively decoupled in HEAs?
What are the strain rate, temperature, and processing limits within which the proposed dislocation pinning and turbulence mechanisms remain dominant?
How do controlled variations in local atomic order (from nearly random to pronounced order) influence the activation barriers for dislocation motion across different HEA systems?
What is the role of thermally activated processes at low strain rates in modifying these strengthening mechanisms?
opportunities: Design controlled comparisons between samples processed to have different degrees of local chemical order (e.g., via annealing treatments) while keeping composition constant.
Perform in-situ mechanical testing combined with high-resolution microscopy (e.g., TEM, STEM) to directly visualize dislocation behavior and pinning at local heterogeneities.
Integrate thermodynamic predictions based on binary mixing enthalpies with experimental tuning of local order to systematically vary the energy landscape affecting dislocations.
Explore the effects of varying strain rates and temperatures to delineate the limits within which mechanisms like dislocation turbulence and heterogeneous strain pinning govern hardness and strength.
Establish quantitative metrics for local shear-fault energy fluctuations and correlate them with macroscopic mechanical properties as a test for the proposed mechanistic hypothesis.

directions.direction: Composition design by varying atomic size mismatch to modulate heterogeneous lattice strain fields.
directions.assessment: Directly targets the hypothesis that heterogeneous lattice strains impede dislocation motion. The physics of size-mismatch induced strain fields is well documented (see PMC9231497::web::000::abstract and PMC9231497::web::002::body). The approach is experimentally feasible by substituting larger atoms (e.g., Ta instead of a more size‐matched element) while keeping the phase and grain size constant.

directions.direction: Thermomechanical processing to control the degree of local chemical order (LCO) in HEAs.
directions.assessment: This method addresses the role of LCO in hardening and strength by annealing or quenching treatments. Literature (PMC6687833::web::000::abstract, PMC10265979::web::000::abstract) indicates LCO alters fault energies and dislocation activation barriers. It is both feasible and informative via controlled annealing experiments.

directions.direction: Modeling and simulation of local shear-fault energy fluctuations to interpret wavy dislocation configurations.
directions.assessment: Leveraging molecular dynamics and discrete dislocation dynamics simulations can directly decouple the role of spatial fluctuations in shear-fault energy as a mediator of dislocation pinning (see PMC10041143::web::000::abstract). This approach is strongly supported by simulation evidence, though it may require careful calibration against experimental parameters.

directions.direction: In-situ mechanical testing combined with high-resolution microscopy to observe dislocation flow turbulence induced by chemical short-range order (SRO).
directions.assessment: This approach examines real-time dislocation dynamics under varying degrees of SRO. Evidence from PMC10990144 suggests that SRO creates localized stress peaks leading to turbulent dislocation motion. Although challenging, the experiments are feasible with modern TEM techniques and can directly validate the proposed mechanism.

directions.direction: Surface treatments or coatings to locally modify strain fields and validate the sensitivity of dislocation pinning mechanisms.
directions.assessment: While promising for altering near-surface mechanical responses, this approach is less direct in addressing the bulk mechanisms governing hardness and strength. The physics of dislocation pinning by heterogeneous strain fields may be probed in a limited zone, making it less globally informative for HEA behavior.

candidates.intervention: Substitute one or more constituent elements with a larger atomic radius (e.g., adding Ta) to amplify lattice distortion while keeping overall composition and grain size constant.

candidates.intervention: Apply annealing treatments at varied temperatures to promote different degrees of local chemical ordering; for example, a lower-temperature, longer anneal to enhance LCO versus rapid quenching to retain a random state.

candidates.hypothesis: Enhanced fluctuations in local shear-fault energy (LSFE) govern increased hardness and strength by inducing a wavy dislocation configuration and increased pinning.
candidates.intervention: Modify the alloy composition slightly (e.g., altering stoichiometry or introducing minor alloying elements) to intensify local fluctuations in LSFE without changing the overall phase.

candidates.hypothesis: Enhanced fluctuations in local shear-fault energy (LSFE) govern increased hardness and strength by inducing a wavy dislocation configuration that enhances dislocation pinning.
candidates.intervention: Slightly modify the alloy composition (e.g., by adjusting stoichiometry or introducing minor alloying elements) to intensify local fluctuations in LSFE while preserving the overall phase and maintaining constant grain size.
candidates.changes: Included a detailed plan for isolating LSFE fluctuation effects from other microstructural factors (e.g., by maintaining constant grain size and phase) and provided clear advanced characterization strategies (high-resolution TEM, atomistic simulations) to map LSFE. The candidate now addresses potential overlap with other strengthening mechanisms.

minor_issues: Possibility of secondary phase formation is noted but not exhaustively addressed.
fixes: Add systematic phase stability studies (e.g., XRD, TEM, and compositional analysis) to confirm single-phase nature under the proposed substitution.
evidence_needs: Experimental data on how adding large atomic radius elements (e.g., Ta) affects phase stability at the intended concentrations.

minor_issues: Reliance on maintaining perfect single-phase purity may require extra controls to eliminate minor secondary phases.
fixes: Broaden compositional and heat treatment windows to ensure that any emergent phases are detected and minimized.
evidence_needs: Data on the compositional limits where single-phase stability is reliably preserved with larger radius element additions.

minor_issues: Attributing dislocation 'turbulence' strictly to SRO may be complex without comparing other concurrent mechanisms (e.g., twinning or partial dislocation activity).
fixes: Include a reference experiment with minimal SRO to isolate its effect on dislocation behavior from other possible strengthening mechanisms.
evidence_needs: In-situ TEM verification of turbulent dislocation flow specifically correlated with measured SRO levels.

minor_issues: Experimental quantification of LSFE fluctuations over relevant length scales can be challenging.
fixes: Adopt a combined modeling and advanced characterization approach (e.g., atomistic simulations plus site-specific TEM or APT) to validate local shear-fault energy distributions.
evidence_needs: Correlate measured LSFE variations with direct observations of dislocation configurations in TEM to confirm wavy dislocation pinning.

minor_issues: Distinguishing LCO-induced strengthening from other thermally activated transformations (e.g., minor precipitation, grain growth) may be nontrivial.
fixes: Implement careful microstructural controls (e.g., identical grain sizes, comprehensive microstructural characterization) to ensure changes are due to local chemical ordering.
evidence_needs: Direct correlations linking measured LCO intensity (via APT or X-ray scattering) to changes in activation energy for dislocation motion.

minor_issues: The hypothesis could benefit from a more detailed discussion of how to isolate the effects of LCO from other potential strengthening mechanisms, such as minor grain growth or segregation.
fixes: Include a more detailed plan for controlling and quantifying potential confounding variables like grain growth and segregation during annealing.
evidence_needs: Experimental studies or simulations that directly link LCO to increased dislocation activation barriers in NiCoCr alloys.
Prior work quantifying the relationship between LCO and planar fault energies in FCC HEAs.

major_issues: The mechanism of 'dislocation flow turbulence' is not fully established in the literature and may require further validation to confirm its role in enhancing both strength and ductility.
minor_issues: The hypothesis could provide more detail on how to distinguish the effects of SRO from other microstructural changes during thermal processing.
fixes: Provide a clearer explanation of how 'dislocation flow turbulence' is quantified and how it directly correlates with mechanical properties.
evidence_needs: Experimental evidence showing a direct correlation between SRO and dislocation turbulence in FCC HEAs.
Studies that validate the proposed mechanism of dynamic dislocation trapping due to SRO.

minor_issues: The hypothesis could clarify how to ensure that the addition of a large atomic radius element does not inadvertently introduce secondary phases.
fixes: Include a detailed plan for thermodynamic modeling or experimental validation to confirm single-phase stability after compositional changes.
evidence_needs: Experimental data linking atomic size mismatch to heterogeneous lattice strain and its effects on dislocation pinning.
Prior studies demonstrating the mechanical property improvements in HEAs with increased atomic size mismatch.

major_issues: The hypothesis relies heavily on the concept of LSFE fluctuations, which is not yet widely validated or quantified in the literature.
minor_issues: The proposed mechanism could benefit from a clearer explanation of how LSFE fluctuations are measured and how they directly influence dislocation configurations.
fixes: Provide additional experimental or simulation-based evidence to support the role of LSFE fluctuations in dislocation pinning.
evidence_needs: Studies that quantify LSFE fluctuations in FCC HEAs and link them to mechanical properties.
Experimental validation of the wavy dislocation configuration caused by LSFE fluctuations.

minor_issues: The hypothesis could further elaborate on the methods used to ensure that single-phase stability is maintained after compositional changes.
fixes: Include a more detailed discussion of the thermodynamic considerations and experimental techniques used to confirm single-phase stability.
evidence_needs: Experimental validation of the relationship between atomic size mismatch and heterogeneous lattice strain in FCC HEAs.
Studies demonstrating the absence of secondary phases in HEAs with increased atomic size mismatch.

major_issues: The hypothesis relies heavily on the assumption that dislocation flow turbulence is the primary mechanism governing strength and ductility, which may not be universally applicable.
minor_issues: The predicted outcome of a 20% increase in yield strength could be considered somewhat arbitrary without further justification.
fixes: Provide additional theoretical or experimental evidence to support the dislocation flow turbulence mechanism.
Offer a more detailed explanation for the predicted 20% increase in yield strength.
evidence_needs: Experimental data demonstrating the relationship between chemical short-range order and dislocation flow turbulence in high-entropy alloys.
Theoretical models or simulations that can predict the effect of dislocation flow turbulence on strength and ductility.

minor_issues: The hypothesis could benefit from a more detailed discussion on how local chemical order affects dislocation activation barriers.
fixes: Provide additional information on the theoretical basis for how local chemical order influences dislocation motion.
Discuss potential limitations or boundary conditions for the proposed mechanism.
